note: Each finding is quoted in the report's own terms. Where the report itself could not be opened from the editing sandbox, checkedVia lists the coverage the figures were checked against; two independent outlets agreeing is the floor.

studies.title: Poverty and Equity Brief: India (June 2025 update, new international poverty lines)
studies.finding: Extreme poverty at $3.00 a day (2021 prices) fell from 27.1% in 2011–12 to 5.3% in 2022–23. On the old $2.15 line, from 16.2% to 2.3% — about 171 million people. At the $4.20 lower-middle-income line, from 57.7% to 23.9%.
studies.caveat: The 2022–23 consumption survey changed its method, and critics argue the comparison with 2011–12 overstates the fall. The Bank's own range on comparable assumptions is still a large decline.

studies.title: Multidimensional Poverty in India since 2005-06 (discussion paper)
studies.finding: The share of Indians in multidimensional poverty — deprived in health, education and living standards — fell from 29.17% in 2013–14 to 11.28% in 2022–23: 24.82 crore people.
studies.caveat: A discussion paper, not an official statistic. Its 2013–14 and 2022–23 values are projected from the trend between NFHS rounds, not surveyed in those years, and it is the government's own think tank.

studies.publisher: UNDP and Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative
studies.title: Global Multidimensional Poverty Index 2023
studies.finding: About 415 million Indians left multidimensional poverty between 2005–06 and 2019–21; the share fell from 55.1% to 16.4%. India was one of 25 countries to halve its index within 15 years.
studies.caveat: The period straddles two governments: roughly 275 million of the exits came between 2005–06 and 2015–16, and about 140 million between 2015–16 and 2019–21.

studies.publisher: Press Information Bureau, Government of India
studies.title: India among the world's most equal societies (citing the World Bank's Spring 2025 Poverty and Equity Brief)
studies.finding: India's consumption Gini of 25.5 in 2022–23, down from 28.8 in 2011–12, would rank it fourth-most equal among the countries compared, behind the Slovak Republic, Slovenia and Belarus.
studies.caveat: The ranking compares India's consumption Gini with other countries' income Ginis, which run higher by construction. The World Bank's own brief notes inequality may be underestimated.

studies.title: PIB's claim that India is fourth most equal country citing World Bank data is misleading
studies.finding: The fourth-most-equal ranking sets a consumption-based Gini beside income-based ones, and the World Bank brief it cites cautions that India's inequality may be underestimated by its data.

studies.publisher: World Inequality Lab (Bharti, Chancel, Piketty, Somanchi)
studies.title: Income and Wealth Inequality in India, 1922–2023: The Rise of the Billionaire Raj
studies.finding: The top 1% took 22.6% of national income in 2022–23 — the highest share since the series began in 1922 — and held 40.1% of wealth, the highest since 1961.
studies.caveat: Built from tax data, national accounts and surveys with strong assumptions; the authors call their estimates a lower bound because India's data are poor. It measures income at the top; the Gini above measures consumption across everyone.

studies.title: Global Innovation Index 2025
studies.finding: India ranked 38th of 139 economies, up from 39th in 2024 and 81st in 2015 — first among lower-middle-income economies.
studies.caveat: Strongest on knowledge and technology outputs; weaker on institutions and business sophistication, where it ranks around 58th and 64th.

studies.title: AI Index Report 2025
studies.finding: India had the highest year-on-year growth in AI hiring (33.4%), ranked second for AI skill penetration (2.5, against 2.6 for the United States), and made 19.9% of contributions to AI projects on GitHub in 2024, second to the US at 23.4%.
studies.caveat: Skill penetration and hiring growth are measured on LinkedIn members, a narrow and urban slice of India's workforce.
